list.listitem: In the acute setting, TBI management focuses on rapid identification of patients at risk for intracranial injury, prevention of secondary brain injury, and early neurosurgical consultation when indicated. Avoid hypoxia, hypotension, hypercarbia, fever, hypoglycemia, and delayed recognition of expanding intracranial hemorrhage.C
Patients with moderate to severe TBI benefit from coordinated trauma, neurosurgical, critical care, rehabilitation, behavioral health, and postacute follow-up systems..C

TBI should be considered both an acute injury and, for many patients, a chronic disease with potential cognitive, behavioral, psychiatric, functional, and caregiver impacts requiring longitudinal primary care coordination.B

background.definition: TBI is a traumatically induced structural injury and/or physiological disruption of brain function as a result of an external force. TBI may be indicated by any of the following: loss or decrease in consciousness, loss of memory surrounding the injury, any change in mental state at the time of injury, neurological deficits, or an intracranial lesion.

list.listitem: In the United States, there were approximately 214,110 TBI-related hospitalizations in 2020 and 68,663 TBI-related deaths in 2023, representing more than 586 TBI-related hospitalizations and 190 TBI-related deaths per day. These estimates do not include TBIs treated only in emergency departments, primary care, urgent care, or those that go untreated..
Globally, approximately 50 to 60 million people experience a TBI each ye.
People aged 75 years and older have the highest numbers and rates of TBI-related hospitalization and death.
Males are nearly twice as likely to be hospitalized and three times more likely to die from TBI than females.
5.3 million living with a long-term TBI-related disability.
An estimated 32% of military personnel evacuated from the war zone in Iraq and Afghanistan had TBI.
TBI has substantial direct medical, rehabilitation, caregiver, lost productivity, and societal costs. A 2016 US analysis estimated $40.6 billion in medical costs attributable to nonfatal TBI.
There were 2.5 million TBI cases in 2010. 87% treated and released from ED, 11% hospitalized, 2% resulted in death.
In the US in 2020, there were 214,000 hospitalizations.
Falls are the leading cause of TBI (35%), with the highest rates for children between the ages of 0 and 14 years (54%) and adults >65 years (79%).
Intentional self-harm, motor vehicle crashes, and assaults are important causes of TBI-related death, with the leading mechanism varying by age group..

Leading cause of TBI related deaths is dependent on age group, with highest rates in individuals >75 years. In general, motor vehicle accidents and self-inflicted injuries/suicide are the leading causes of TBI related deaths in the overall population. However, by age, the leading causes of TBI related deaths are: 0-4 y/o: Assaults 5-24 y/o: Motor vehicle crashes 25-64 y/o: Intentional self-harm >65 y/o: Falls

In military populations, blast exposure is an important mechanism of TBI, especially in deployed settings; other mechanisms include falls, motor vehicle crashes, sports or training injuries, assaults, bullets, and fragments..

TBI is heterogeneous. Primary brain injury occurs at the time of trauma and includes focal injuries such as contusion, epidural hematoma, subdural hematoma, subarachnoid hemorrhage, intracerebral hemorrhage, penetrating injury, and diffuse axonal injury. Secondary brain injury develops after the initial trauma and may result from hypoxia, hypotension, hypercarbia, fever, hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia, cerebral edema, ischemia, seizures, coagulopathy, and increased intracranial pressure..
Primary brain injury- Focal damage, typically from contact injuries, can result in cortical contusion, subdural hematoma, epidural hematoma, subarachnoid hemorrhage, and intracerebral hemorrhage.
Diffuse axonal injury results from acceleration-deceleration, rotational, and complex pressure wave forces.
Secondary brain injury- Delayed complications include brain edema, ischemia, increased intracranial pressure, hypoxia, and hypertensive episodes leading to further neuropathologic damage.
Primary prevention, such as seat belt and helmet use, reduces the risk of TBI.C
Helmet wear reduces overall risk of TBI and the severity of head trauma.
Non-legislative interventions such as community-based education and free helmets can increase observed helmet use in children.
Proper use of protective equipment in military, athletic, and recreational activities may reduce the incidence and severity of brain injury.
Improving strength, gait, and balance through physical therapy reduces falls and head trauma in the elderly.
Safety proofing homes for children and the elderly may reduce TBI risk due to falls.
Seat belt and child safety seat use reduces incidence and severity of brain injury due to motor vehicle accident.
Patients with a history of acquired or developmental brain impairment should be counseled to reduce their TBI risk exposure through activity modification/avoidance.
Patients with a history of TBI should be screened for co-morbid chemical dependency and, if present, undergo treatment.

TBI severity is commonly classified using Glasgow Coma Scale score, duration of loss or alteration of consciousness, duration of post-traumatic amnesia, focal neurologic deficits, and neuroimaging findings.B

In acute evaluation, noncontrast head CT is the cornerstone first-line imaging test for patients at risk for clinically important intracranial injury. MRI is more sensitive than CT for some traumatic intracranial injuries, but it is generally used for persistent unexplained deficits, subacute symptoms, prognostication, or when CT is negative but clinical concern remains. SORT C
Early CT/MRI should be done in patients with moderate or severe TBI to determine if surgery is needed.C
A negative head CT does not rule out TBI, especially mild TBI/concussion. SORT C
Initial assessment involves the GCS. In the acute setting, symptoms of moderate to severe TBI include LOC lasting longer than 30 minutes and a GCS less than 13 minutes (see ).

Initial assessment includes the Glasgow Coma Scale, pupillary examination, focal neurologic examination, assessment for skull or basilar skull fracture, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, seizure, intoxication, mechanism of injury, duration of loss or alteration of consciousness, and duration of post-traumatic amnesia. Moderate to severe TBI is suggested by GCS <13, prolonged loss of consciousness or post-traumatic amnesia, focal neurologic deficit, seizure, penetrating injury, depressed or basilar skull fracture, or abnormal neuroimaging.
In addition, the finding of posttraumatic amnesia greater than 24 hours is suggestive of moderate/severe TBI.
Intoxication can hamper determination of severity in the acute setting.
In the post-acute setting, survivors of moderate/severe TBI can be unreliable historians of personal medical information, stressing the need for collateral reporting from family/caregivers.

Absent venous pulsations are very sensitive for detecting increased intracranial pressure, but are nonspecific. Findings that significantly increase the likelihood of clinically significant findings on head loss of consciousness (LOC), CT include LOC, especially if >5 minutes; decreasing LOC; penetrating skull injury or palpable depressed skull fracture; and signs of basilar skull fracture.
Physical signs suspicious for skull fracture greatly increase the likelihood of severe intracranial injury (LR+ = 16).

Patients with suspected moderate or severe TBI, focal neurologic deficit, seizure, depressed or basilar skull fracture, penetrating injury, persistent altered mental status, anticoagulant use, or clinical deterioration require urgent noncontrast head CT and neurosurgical evaluation when abnormalities are found. MRI may be considered when CT is negative but clinical concern persists, when symptoms or deficits are unexplained, or in the subacute/chronic setting..
Diffusion tensor imaging, an advanced form of MRI, does not aid the diagnosis of TBI.
Early imaging can help provide prompt surgical intervention if needed.

Blood-based biomarkers such as GFAP and UCH-L1 may help rule out the need for head CT in selected adults with suspected mild TBI who have GCS 13–15, meet clinical criteria for CT by a decision rule, and are judged to have low but nonzero risk of traumatic intracranial hemorrhage. Biomarkers should be used as adjuncts to, not replacements for, clinical assessment and validated CT decision rules. In a 2022 cohort study, GFAP plus UCH-L1 had 100% sensitivity but only 25% specificity for CT lesions, compared with 100% sensitivity and 33% specificity for the Canadian CT Head Rule. SORT B.
Baseline assessments are required by organizations such as the NCAA for athletes, but are probably of limited value based on a large retrospective cohort study.

Clinical decisions rules such as the Canadian CT Head Rule, New Orleans Criteria (>60 years old), and Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) Head Injury Trauma algorithm apply more to mild TBI cases. They have been well validated for deciding which patients with minor head injury and normal or near-normal GCS require head CT.
Absence of all features on the Canadian CT Head Rule, New Orleans Criteria and PECARN Head Injury Trauma algorithm makes severe intracranial injury very unlikely.
The Glasgow Coma Score is used to assess the severity of traumatic brain injury.
A clinical decision rule is modestly useful to determine which children will have persistent post-concussive symptoms after acute concussion.
The Infant Scalp Score can identify a large group of infants with a very low risk of clinically important TBI.
In children, use a validated pediatric decision rule such as PECARN to guide CT use and reduce unnecessary radiation exposure. SORT B

For adults taking anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents who have a normal baseline neurologic examination and an initial CT without hemorrhage, do not routinely repeat CT or admit/observe solely because of anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, unless other clinical criteria for monitoring are present. SORT B
See for a suggested approach to diagnosis and management of TBI.

Acute TBI management prioritizes prevention of secondary brain injury: maintain oxygenation, ventilation, blood pressure, cerebral perfusion, normothermia, glucose control, and timely neurosurgical intervention when indicate C
For moderate to severe TBI, use protocolized trauma/neurocritical care with serial neurologic examinations, repeat imaging when clinically indicated, and ICP monitoring in selected patients. SORT C

After medical stabilization, patients with moderate to severe TBI often require coordinated inpatient rehabilitation and structured transition to outpatient rehabilitation, behavioral health, primary care, caregiver support, and community reintegration services.C

Mild TBI/concussion management should include education, avoidance of reinjury, gradual return to cognitive and physical activity after brief rest, and follow-up for patients at risk for persistent symptoms. SORT B.

Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended solely for intubation, external ventricular drain or intraparenchymal ICP monitor placement, basilar skull fracture, CSF leak, or pneumocephalus. Use perioperative prophylaxis for neurosurgical procedures according to local surgical prophylaxis protocols. For open or penetrating skull fractures, broad-spectrum antibiotics with good CNS penetration may be considered for a short course, with surgical debridement and irrigation when indicated. SORT C
Corticosteroids are not recommended for improving outcome or reducing ICP in acute TBI because they increase mortality. SORT A.

Low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin 40 mg daily) or low-dose unfractionated heparin (heparin 5000 units three times daily) should be used for DVT prophylaxis. There is a risk of expanding an intracranial hemorrhage.
Levetiracetam, dosed to therapeutic levels (500-1000 mg every 12 hours for seven days), may be used to decrease the incidence of posttraumatic seizures within 7 days of injury.

Based on a meta-analysis of observational data, early seizure prophylaxis may be useful in mild and moderate TBI. The most widely studied anticonvulsants were levetiracetam, phenytoin, and valproic acid. In the studies, the rate of post-traumatic seizures ranged from 0% to 4%. The overall absolute risk reduction was 0.6% (95% CI 0.1% - 1.2%, NNT = 167). For patients with mild injuries, the ARR was also 0.6% (0.01% - 1.2%). Since seizures are uncommon and the NNT so high, the benefits should be balanced against the harms.

Mannitol can be used for control of raised ICP at doses of 0.25 to 1 g/kg every 4 to 6 hours as needed in those patients who have not responded to initial measures such as CSF drainage, analgesia and sedation. A Cochrane review concluded that it may reduce mortality compared with pentobarbital, but did not improve outcomes compared with hypertonic saline. ICP directed treatment may be beneficial. Consider hypertonic saline first due to complications of mannitol therapy (although a Cochrane review concluded that there was no clear evidence of greater efficacy of hypertonic saline compared with mannitol).

High-dose barbiturate administration is considered only in the setting of unresponsive ICP. Although effective for the control of ICP, the use of barbiturate coma has not shown to improve outcomes following TBI and pentobarbital infusions are associated with morbidity. A Cochrane review concluded that there is no evidence that barbiturates for acute severe head injury improve patient outcomes, and frequently causes a fall in blood pressure that may offset the effect of lowering ICP.

There is no data to support the use of magnesium, mild hypothermia, beta-2 receptor antagonists following acute TBI to reduce mortality or disability following TBI. Cochrane reports that the use of progesterone requires more study. There is insufficient evidence to support the use of progesterone, and an RCT found no benefit at 6 months from use of progesterone in the acute setting.

The CRASH-3 study randomized 12,737 patients with TBI to tranexamic acid or placebo, with 72% treated within 3 hours of injury. The likelihood of death due to head injury was lower with tranexamic acid in patients with mild-to-moderate head injury (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0·64-0·95) but not in patients with severe head injury (RR 0.99). The absolute risk difference for patients with mild to moderate TBI was 1.7% for an NNT of 59. A Cochrane review also concluded that tranexamic acid given within 3 hours safely reduces mortality in patients with traumatic hemorrhage based on a meta-analysis of 2 studies with over 20,000 patients that predated CRASH-3.

Six RCTs with 1862 patients studied calcium channel blockers for patients with acute TBI. The reviewers found that the primary benefit was with nimodipine in the subgroup of TBI patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage.
There is conflicting evidence on the benefit of a liberal transfusion strategy compared to a restrictive strategy in critically ill patients with traumatic brain injury.
A Cochrane review concluded that there is no evidence to support the use of excitatory amino acid inhibitors such as glutamate.
There is no proven pharmacologic intervention for treatment of post-TBI agitation and aggression or cognitive deficits.
A systematic review of reviews evaluating the safety and efficacy of pharmacologic treatments, recommended avoiding benzodiazepines and haloperidol in treatment of agitation/aggression after TBI.
Another systematic review of medications to improve cognitive function after TBI found evidence of a small effect for methylphenidate (Cohen's d = 0.34).

Based on a systematic review, chronic headaches occur in 57.8% of patients following TBI, especially in those with preexisting headache syndromes and with mild TBI (75.3%). Pain medication for recurrent headaches should begin with acetaminophen and NSAIDs at standard doses.
Chronic pain is also common. In individuals with noncombat injuries, the prevalence of chronic pain was 51.5% and in combat-associated brain injuries, 43.1%.
Use of anticonvulsants like phenytoin or valproate to prevent late posttraumatic seizure is not recommended.
Sertraline reduces the risk of depression in patients after traumatic brain injury (NNT = 6).
In the acute setting, prompt neurosurgical intervention when indicated is associated with improved outcomes with TBI.
In severe TBI, a policy of closely monitoring intracranial pressure and maintaining pressure at less than 20 mm Hg or less is not superior to monitoring with imaging and clinical examination alone.
Decompressive craniectomy may be useful in patients with traumatic brain injury and intracranial hypertension.
A Cochrane review found no evidence from RCTs to support the routine use of secondary decompressive craniectomy to reduce unfavorable outcomes in adults with severe TBI and refractory high ICP.

An inpatient rehabilitation phase should follow the acute hospitalization for most moderate/severe TBI cases. Inpatient rehabilitation should be multidisciplinary and guided by the patient's current level of functioning. See .
A Cochrane review concluded that there is weak evidence to support neurorehabilitation for symptoms of anxiety in patients with mild to moderate TBI.

After inpatient rehabilitation, ongoing outpatient cognitive treatment should involve treating impaired attention/concentration, learning and memory difficulties, executive control dysfunction, and communication problems.
Vocational training is often needed in cases of severe TBI. Peer mentoring may also be beneficial.
It is unclear if fitness training improves cardiorespiratory conditioning after traumatic brain injury.
Early onset and more intensive neurorehabilitation promotes functional recovery of patients with moderate to severe TBI.
A systematic review of 10 RCTs found that enforced bedrest did not improve outcomes in children with concussion; activity should be guided by symptoms as tolerated.
A study randomized 367 patients with mild TBI to prescribed light exercise 30 minutes per day or recommendation for a gradual return to exercise. There was no difference in outcomes between groups.

A study randomized 125 age 12 5o 25 years with acute concussion, GCS 15, and normal imaging. They were randomized to instruction to avoid video screens for 48 hours or not. They found that recovery was greater in the no screeens group (60% vs 72%, NNT = 8, p < 0.05). Those in the control group also took longer to recover.
Avoid cognitively impairing medications.
Cognitive behavioral therapy showed some effectiveness in treatment of acute stress disorder following TBI.

Multiple psychological interventions, including cognitive-behavioral, family/marital, and group therapy, can be helpful in addressing the emotional and behavioral problems which follow TBI. The most common problems are aggression and agitation.
Concussion is associated with an increased risk of future suicide.
Mild traumatic brain injury is associated with an increase in behavioral and affective disorders in children.
Full caloric replacement should be started by day 7 post injury.
Graduated compression stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression stockings are recommended in the absence of a lower extremity injury.
There is no high quality evidence that hypothermia is beneficial in the treatment of head injury.
There is inadequate data to support the use of hyperbaric oxygen therapy.
A recent RCT showed no improvement from hyperbaric oxygen therapy for post-concussive symptoms in service members.
The benefit of acupuncture for acute management or rehabilitation is uncertain.
The post-acute phase of TBI treatment is typically lifelong with the primary care physician serving as the care coordinator.
After inpatient rehabilitation, primary care physicians will likely need to refer patients to multiple specialties.
Neuropsychologists can provide cognitive testing and recommendations if further cognitive therapy is indicated.
Outpatient physical, occupational, and speech therapy may be indicated to further restore independent activities of daily living (IADL).
Pain management and neurology consultations can be a resource for chronic post-traumatic headaches.
Substance abuse programs are indicated if positive history of abuse.
Patients unable to perform IADLs safely may need referral for assisted living.

Blood pressure should be monitored with the goal of avoiding systolic pressures <90 mm Hg, although guidelines suggest maintaining the systolic pressure >100 mm Hg for patients 50 to 69 years old and >110 mm Hg for patients 15 to 49 or >70 years old.
Oxygenation should be monitored with the goal of PaO2 >60 mm Hg, avoid SpO2 of <90.
Prophylactic hypothermia does not decrease mortality when compared with normothermic controls.

ICP monitoring should be done in all patients with a GCS of 3 to 8 after resuscitation and abnormal CT findings including hematomas, contusions, edema, herniations, or compressed basal cisterns. Also consider monitoring in patients with severe TBI, normal head CT, and two or more of following: age >40 years, motor posturing, or BP <90 mm Hg.

An ICP above 20 mm Hg should be treated. Targeting a goal cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) of 50 to 60 mm Hg appears to reduce morbidity and mortality. However, trying to keep CPP above 70 mm Hg with fluids and pressors increases the risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome.
Monitoring ICP does not reduce mortality but may improve electrolyte imbalances, rate of renal failure, and increase favorable functional outcomes.
The course of recovery is highly individualized and depends on the type and degree of injury, as well as other factors.C
Patients with moderate injuries can often function independently, but are at increased risk of psychiatric illness.B
Patients with severe injuries are unlikely to return to work or reach full independence.B
Without multidisciplinary inpatient rehabilitation, cognitive deficits are likely to be more numerous and severe.
Following TBI, patients are at increased risk for psychiatric illness.
Unless behavioral problems are addressed, patients are likely to have difficulty with interpersonal relationships.
Patients with moderate to severe TBI remain at increased risk for seizures.
Half of patients with mild TBI will experience at least four post-concussive symptoms one year later and 1 in 10 patients will have very low level of cognitive function one year after injury.

Poorer outcome has been associated with age >55 years, poorer pre-injury function, longer duration coma, brain stem abnormalities, lower motor score on the GCS, elevated ICP, prolonged PTA, intracranial mass lesion, and low functioning abilities at start of rehabilitation.
A meta-analysis of studies in military veterans with TBI found an association with all-cause dementia and vascular dementia but not Alzheimer dementia.
A prospective cohort study concluded that intelligence was not affected by mild concussion.

The majority of individuals with moderate injuries can function independently and often return to work. However, most continue to show cognitive and personality problems associated with frontal and temporal damage.

Individuals with severe injuries are unlikely to return to work or live independently. They continue to express persistent cognitive and motor slowness, poor memory, and executive control dysfunction. They are at four to five times greater risk for developing dementia.
Neuropsychological evaluations in the chronic recovery period are helpful in determining the presence of permanent cognitive problems and their effect on daily functioning.
Children do not benefit from seizure prophylaxis unless they experienced an immediate post-injury seizure.
